input.rationale: Coverage check on the verification finding, done by reading the two captured tests that exercise VerifyLeader. TestRaft_VerifyLeader_PartialConnect uses a three-voter cluster with one follower disconnected and expects success, because a voter quorum of two remains reachable; TestRaft_VerifyLeader_Fail forces a follower to a higher term so the leader steps down and expects ErrNotLeader or ErrLeadershipLost. Neither test introduces a non-voter, so the captured suite neither contradicts nor covers the acknowledgement path this finding rests on. The account gains that as counterevidence with the test lines as a source; no execution or conclusion changes.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: leader verification can be satisfied without a voter quorum, and the resulting incorrect answer is available for about one lease interval before the same node stops leading. Evidence: in the latest receipt the slowed-timer setup event 22 records three voters with a quorum of two, a voter unreachable by direct AppendEntries and a reachable non-voter, and its result event 23 records verification succeeding with no error in under a millisecond while the node still led; events 25 and 26 repeat the premise and the same result with the repository's default in-memory timers; the bound events 24 and 27 record the node becoming a follower after 1012 ms with a 1000 ms lease and after 60 ms with the default 50 ms lease. Mechanism from source: verifyLeader starts its count at one for itself and registers the future in every entry of the leader's replication map, which startStopReplication builds for every server of the configuration except the leader without filtering by suffrage; each peer's heartbeat acknowledges the pending verification on a successful AppendEntries, so a non-voter's acknowledgement raises the count to the voter quorum computed from voters alone, while the lease check counts voters only and therefore closes the window about one lease interval later. The documented purpose of the call, anchored, is to ensure the peer is still the leader and to prevent returning stale data from the FSM after leadership is lost, which is what a non-voter acknowledgement cannot establish. Coverage: the captured tests that exercise this call use voter-only clusters, so nothing in the snapshot pins the non-voter path either way.
counterevidence: The measured bound limits the impact: the node stops reporting itself as leader about one lease interval after losing the voter quorum, so the incorrect verification result is available only inside that interval.

The defect requires a configuration containing non-voters; in a voters-only cluster every replication peer is a voter and the acknowledgement set equals the voter set, so the path cannot diverge from the voter quorum. The captured verification tests are exactly that shape: a three-voter cluster with one follower disconnected expects success because a voter quorum remains reachable, and a forced higher term on a follower expects ErrNotLeader or ErrLeadershipLost.
No write path is affected: entry commitment uses the commitment map, which contains voters only, so this is a read-verification path rather than a commit-rule path.

The probe calls VerifyLeader directly rather than through an application that then serves a read, so the stale-read consequence is argued from the anchored documentation rather than measured end to end.
limitations: Measured on four-peer in-memory clusters with the repository's own facilities; production timings and transports are not covered.
The bound is reported for the two timer configurations used (1000 ms and the default 50 ms lease) and depends on the lease timeout, not on a fixed wall-clock constant.
Both cases isolate the leader by transport disconnection and confirm it with direct AppendEntries attempts recorded in the same events.
interpretations.joint_history: Three receipts answer this question. The first (5e092a2b160b4a2f955d48ee6fa06ad9 at indices 22 and 23) measured the isolation with slowed timers; the second (c0f7723f05d8430aaf36bf2b4f9ce862 at 22-25) ran it with slowed and default timers; the third (7401ab5a8f7c4cd69d947e972ea31a61 at 22-27) repeats both cases and measures when the isolated leader stops reporting itself as leader.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft's configuration scan excludes committed configuration entries. restoreFromCommittedLogs clamps the store's commit index and calls processLogs, which ends with setLastApplied(index); the following scan loop iterates from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 up to the last log index, so any configuration entry with index at or below the recovered commit index is never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry. Both staging producers cap the staged value at entries already stored (raft.go:1266 for the leader, raft.go:1558 for followers), so the recovered commit index reaches a configuration entry whenever later entries were stored after it was committed. Consequence: the restarted node's r.configurations is the snapshot's configuration or, with no snapshot, empty, while its log reports that configuration entry as committed; an empty configuration makes runFollower abort elections (raft.go:232) and leaves the node's participant eligibility wrong until a later configuration entry or installed snapshot repairs it. Construction feedback: local, non-retained runs of these harness bytes reported variant A with last_applied_after_restart=11, config_scan_start_index=12, the bootstrap LogConfiguration at index 1 not covered and latest_config_after_restart_len=0; variant B reported the committed LogConfiguration at index 23 (adding nonvoter-B) not covered with the post-restart configuration reduced to the snapshot's single voter. Those local numbers are construction feedback only, so the conclusion stays conditional until the retained receipt of the queued experiment is read.
counterevidence: The recovered committed entries are still applied to the FSM (processLogs), and a node can still learn the current configuration from any later configuration entry or installed snapshot, so the omission can be repaired and does not by itself corrupt the FSM.

Snapshot-level configuration is loaded correctly by restoreSnapshot, so the omission only appears for configuration entries that sit between the last snapshot (or index 0) and the recovered commit index.
No captured test asserts configuration state after a RestoreCommittedLogs restart, so the captured suite neither confirms nor contradicts the omission.
limitations: The account applies only to nodes configured with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and a log store implementing CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag off, lastApplied equals the snapshot index and the scan range is unchanged.
The consequences on elections, quorum and participant eligibility are currently source-derived (hasVote and the runFollower election gate), not measured.
The exact reported field values and the runtime confirmation depend on the queued experiment's retained receipt.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft's configuration scan excludes committed configuration entries, and the retained execution shows it. restoreFromCommittedLogs clamps the store's commit index, applies the recovered range through processLogs (which ends with setLastApplied(index)), and the following scan loop starts at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so a configuration entry at or below the recovered commit index is never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry. Staging producers cap the staged value at entries already stored, so the recovered commit index reaches a configuration entry whenever later entries were written after it committed. Parsed event 0 (event restore_committed_logs_no_snapshot, receipt 5e1ce9aa430842d5a9325cfecbc885f6): staged commit index 11 equals lastApplied 11, scan start 12, the committed LogConfiguration at index 1 is outside the scan, and the node's latest configuration after restart is empty (length 0) although before restart it held one voter and the FSM had been fed up to index 11. interpretations.rationale: Current account: a RestoreCommittedLogs restart cannot complete startup recovery once the recovered committed range needs more FSM batches than the 128-slot fsmMutateCh, because runFSM is only started after the recovery work that feeds it. The receipt shows both the boundary and the mechanism. Parsed event 3 (variant committed-range-entries-6001, 94 batches): NewRaft returned in 6 ms with lastApplied 6001, i.e. the same code path completes when the range fits the buffer, and that node's configuration after restart was empty (length 0), matching the separate configuration-scan account. Parsed event 5 (variant committed-range-entries-9001, 141 batches): no return within the 20000 ms bound, and the frames captured at that moment are goroutine 10 [select] github.com/hashicorp/raft.(*Raft).processLogs.func1 -> (*Raft).processLogs(index 0x2329 = 9001) -> (*Raft).restoreFromCommittedLogs -> NewRaft, created by the harness restart goroutine. No runFSM goroutine exists for that instance, so no consumer can drain the buffer and no repair is enabled by time alone; the only escape in that select is the instance's own shutdown channel, which nothing closes during construction. Conditions: RestoreCommittedLogs enabled with a commit-tracking store, and a recovered commit index whose distance from the last applied/snapshot index exceeds 8192 authored entries (128 batches of 64) - for example a snapshot gap larger than 8192 entries on a node that crashed before the next snapshot, or a node with snapshotting disabled. Fault assumptions: none injected; the block follows from the retained history produced by the node's own commit path.
counterevidence: The observation is a 20000 ms bounded wait, so the account claims a blocked startup under the stated conditions, not an infinite block proven for all time; a caller that closes the instance's shutdown channel could release the select.

The two cases differ only in the amount of authored history (6000 versus 9000 commands) and used a single-node in-memory cluster with an InmemCommitTrackingStore and snapshotting disabled, so the boundary is a batch-capacity property of NewRaft rather than a measured property of production stores.

The blocked range here was recovered from the same node's own log without any snapshot; whether a production restart reaches a range above 8192 entries depends on snapshot cadence and crash timing, which were not measured.
limitations: Applies only when Config.RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a LogStore implementing CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag off, NewRaft never calls processLogs before starting runFSM.
The threshold is expressed in MaxAppendEntries-sized batches against the 128-slot buffer, so a configuration with a different MaxAppendEntries moves the boundary proportionally.
Interaction with the configuration-scan gap (both appear in the same recovery sequence) is not separated by this experiment; each is independently witnessed.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the empty configuration produced by a RestoreCommittedLogs restart removes the membership admission check from vote and pre-vote handling, and the retained execution shows the resulting admission of a non-member. Parsed event 6 (setup): live_config_after_restart is empty with live_voters 0 and derived_quorum_size 1, while log_recorded_config still holds the one bootstrapped voter, so the configuration in force (recorded in the node's own log) is not what the node uses. Parsed event 7 (result, same node and configuration): request_vote_granted=true with request_vote_term 3, request_prevote_granted=true with request_prevote_term 4, candidate_in_live_config=false, node_term_after_requests 3 - that is, a candidate appearing in no configuration was granted a vote and a pre-vote, and the node adopted the requester's higher term. Both declared comparisons are violated at index 7. Mechanism from source: requestVote and requestPreVote reject candidates outside the configuration only when the handler's own Servers list is non-empty, a leniency documented for the bootstrap case, so an empty list accepts any candidate; quorumSize() over the empty voter list yields 1. Consequence boundaries: the requester's log was made at least as recent as the node's, so no recency rule applied, and the restarted node has no known leader after its own recovery, so the leader-availability rejection did not apply either; the node's own election gating (runFollower aborting when no peers are known) is source-derived, not measured, and is left as the next discriminator.
counterevidence: Granting a vote when the configuration is empty is intentional behaviour for a cluster that is being bootstrapped; the defect here is that the node's own recovery path leaves the configuration empty in a cluster that is not being bootstrapped, not the leniency itself.

The probe supplied a candidate whose log was at least as recent as the node's and whose term was higher, which is what makes the vote grant observable; a stale or older candidate would still be rejected by the log-recency rules.
The same configuration gap is repaired by any later configuration entry or installed snapshot, so a healthy cluster with continuing traffic repairs the node without operator action.
limitations: Measured on a single-node in-memory cluster with snapshotting disabled and the repository's InmemCommitTrackingStore, with the candidate reaching the node through the in-memory transport.

Only RequestVote and RequestPreVote admission was driven; whether the node accepts AppendEntries or accepts leadership from a non-member, and whether its own candidacy is suppressed, is not measured here.
The node adopted the requester's term, but no consequence of that term change (for example disruption of an existing leader) was measured.

interpretations.rationale: Current account (source-derived, measurement pending): a leader's commit rule is computed from r.configurations.latest, which commitment.setConfiguration and quorumSize consume; when a restart leaves that configuration behind the log's committed history, a node that then leads uses the smaller voter set for both its quorum and its replication set, so it can acknowledge a write that a majority of the configuration in force never stores, and a leader elected from that configuration can be elected without the entry. Source side: restoreFromCommittedLogs applies logs up to the recovered commit index and the configuration scan then starts after it, so the recommitted configuration entry is never loaded even though the entry recording the change remains in the log; quorumSize and commitment both count voters from the recovered configuration, and commitment.recalculate commits the (n-1)/2-th match index of that set. The discrimination is the queued experiment: it restarts the node under test from a snapshot that records a three-voter configuration while the configuration in force has five voters, transfers leadership to it, and checks whether the acknowledged write is backed by a true majority and whether it survives in a leader elected from the configuration in force. Local construction feedback of these harness bytes showed the chain end to end, including acknowledged apply error nil with only two holders out of five voters and a later leader without the payload; those local numbers are construction feedback only and are not retained evidence, so the conclusion stays conditional until the receipt is read.
counterevidence: The configuration gap needs a snapshot taken while a smaller configuration was committed plus later entries that advance the recovered commit index past the recommitting entry; a cluster that snapshots after every configuration change may not reach that state.
A later configuration entry or an installed snapshot repairs the recovered configuration, and the experiment deliberately prevents repair by isolating one voter and keeping the configuration stable.
The local construction run is not retained evidence; the phase ordering it exercises (transfer, disconnection, shutdown of holders) could behave differently under the controller's execution.
limitations: Applies to nodes with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and a LogStore implementing CommitTrackingLogStore.

The measured history is a single in-memory five-voter cluster with authored commands and the repository's in-memory stores; production stores, multi-datacenter latencies and concurrent client traffic are not covered.

The acknowledgement is observed through the Apply future of the node under test; the loss is observed as absence of the payload from the later leader's log store, which does not by itself prove that no other surviving node could later resurrect the entry.

interpretations.rationale: Current account (source-derived, probe queued): both public endpoints are pinned to zero. GetConfiguration constructs a local configurationsFuture and assigns configurations{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()}, leaving committed, committedIndex and latestIndex at their zero values, so ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns 0 although the IndexFuture contract says Index holds the index of the applied log entry; Stats then reports s["latest_configuration_index"] = future.Index(), so the documented stat key is always "0" even while s["latest_configuration"] shows the current server set. The captured tests never assert a non-zero index from this future (the only Index() assertion in the captured suite belongs to an Apply result), so nothing contradicts the reading. Local construction feedback of the queued harness reported the committed configuration entry at index 6 with future_index 0 and stats value "0" while the live configuration already contained the nonvoter; that local run is construction feedback only and is not retained evidence, so the account stays conditional until the receipt is read.
counterevidence: A zero index is harmless for callers that only read Configuration(), and GetConfiguration is documented as returning the latest configuration, which may be uncommitted; the contract violation is in the Index the future exposes and in the stat key, not in the configuration content.
The main loop still answers configurationsCh with the full configurations struct, so internal consumers such as snapshotting do see the real indices; only the client-facing future is flattened.
limitations: Observability-only impact: no consensus decision, election, or client write outcome is affected by this reading.

Measured on the captured test facilities with a two-peer cluster; the same construction is used for every GetConfiguration call, so the endpoint does not depend on cluster size, which the probe does not vary.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: both client-facing endpoints are pinned to zero, and the retained execution shows it. Parsed event 13 records a committed LogConfiguration entry at index 6 in a two-peer cluster; parsed event 14, taken in the same state, records future_index 0 with future_index_matches_entry false, stats_latest_configuration_index "0" with stats_index_matches_entry false, and a live configuration that already contains the changed server set (three servers: two voters plus the added nonvoter). Both declared comparisons are violated at index 14. Mechanism from source: GetConfiguration constructs a local configurationsFuture and assigns configurations{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()}, so committed, committedIndex and latestIndex keep their zero values and ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns 0 even though the IndexFuture contract states that Index holds the index of the applied log entry; Stats maps future.Index() into the documented key latest_configuration_index, so that key is a constant while the neighbouring latest_configuration key shows the real server set. The captured suite only asserts a non-zero Index for an Apply result, so nothing in the snapshot contradicts the reading.

Measured on a two-peer in-memory cluster with the captured test facilities; the same construction is used on every call, so the value does not vary with cluster size, which the probe did not vary.

The comparison uses the configuration entry's own future index as the expected reference; that index is itself produced by the library, and the log-store read of the entry type at that index corroborates it.

interpretations.rationale: Current account of the repair side of this question: the configuration gap closes as soon as any configuration entry reaches the node. Parsed event 15 records the restarted node with an empty live configuration while its log records the two voters of the configuration in force; parsed event 16 records that after the serving leader commits AddNonvoter at index 8 the node's live configuration becomes the three servers of the configuration in force (two voters plus the added nonvoter), and config_repaired_by_later_entry is true. So the window opened by the restart is bounded by the next configuration entry or installed snapshot, which is what the earlier account listed as counterevidence; the underlying defect is unchanged, since the node's configuration was empty from NewRaft until that entry arrived, and its own log already recorded the configuration in force. The declared comparison for this receipt could not be resolved because the correlation expected the setup/result pair at indices that do not carry it; the pair is present and complete at indices 15 and 16, which is what this account cites.
counterevidence: This receipt shows the repair path working, which limits the duration of the gap but not the reading that the node was wrong when it started: before the new entry arrived, the node had an empty configuration while its log recorded the configuration in force.
The repair in this receipt required an explicit configuration change; a cluster with no membership churn after the restart would leave the node in the wrong configuration indefinitely.
The comparison for this receipt was recorded as unresolved because of correlation indices, so this account cites the parsed events directly rather than the comparison outcome.
limitations: Measured on a two-peer in-memory cluster with commit-tracking stores and snapshotting disabled; the empty (rather than stale) case is the one exercised.

The repair entry was committed by the surviving leader while the restarted node was still a member of the configuration in force; a node that is itself removed by the missed entry would not receive such an entry in the same way.
Only the arriving-configuration-entry path was measured; the installed-snapshot repair path is source-derived.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the configuration gap makes an acknowledged write unsafe, not merely a stale local view. Parsed event 9 records the restarted node holding the snapshot's three-voter configuration (derived quorum two) while the configuration in force has five voters and its log still holds a configuration entry beyond the snapshot; parsed event 10 records that node becoming leader through the library's own transfer API with the same three-voter configuration and a replication set of two peers; parsed event 11 records an Apply returning nil while only two nodes held the payload, below the three acknowledgements the five-voter configuration in force requires, so the assertion that the acknowledged write is backed by a true majority is violated at index 11; parsed event 12 records a leader elected from the five-voter configuration (term four) whose log store has no entry carrying the payload, so the assertion that the acknowledged write survives is violated at index 12. Mechanism from source: the restart applies logs up to the recovered commit index and the scan then starts after that index, so the recommitted configuration entry never reaches processConfigurationLogEntry; the leader's quorum and commitment set come from that recovered configuration, so commitment.recalculate advances the commit index on the (n-1)/2-th match index of the smaller voter set. The reading at index 12 is payload-based rather than index-based: the later leader reports the same last-applied index the acknowledged entry had, but a different entry occupies it. A later re-run of the same harness file failed its transfer phase before reaching these phases, which is why this account cites the earlier receipt that carries them.
counterevidence: The state needs RestoreCommittedLogs enabled with a commit-tracking store, a snapshot taken while a smaller configuration was committed, and later entries advancing the recovered commit index past the recommitting entry; a cluster that snapshots after every configuration change may not reach it.
Any later configuration entry or an installed snapshot repairs the recovered configuration, so the window closes once the node receives one; the harness prevents that repair deliberately.

Both holders of the acknowledged entry were stopped for the final reading, so the observation establishes absence from the new leader rather than permanent erasure if a stopped holder rejoins; the entry was nevertheless one that a true majority had not stored.
limitations: Measured on one in-memory five-voter cluster with the repository's in-memory transport, commit-tracking store and mock FSM; production stores and network timing are not covered.
The harness orchestrates a leadership transfer, a transport disconnection and the shutdown of the two holders, so the ordering is the harness's, though every step uses public APIs.

A later re-run of the same harness file aborted its transfer phase when the restarted node was already leader, so the account rests on the receipt that completed all phases rather than on repeated runs.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the transfer trigger is not restricted to the current leader, so a non-member can displace a healthy leader. Parsed event 17 records the state before the request: the removed node is not in the configuration in force and the target is a follower. Parsed event 18 records the outcome after the removed node's TimeoutNow arrived: the target became leader, leadership_changed is true, old_leader_stepped_down is true, and the request returned no error. Both declared comparisons are violated at index 18, in a run whose exit code is 0. Mechanism from source: timeoutNow clears the known leader, sets the recipient's state to Candidate and stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer without looking at the request's RPCHeader, so any transport-reachable peer can trigger the exchange; the election that follows sets LeadershipTransfer on its vote requests, and requestVote skips its leader-availability rejection when that flag is set, so voters that already know a healthy leader still grant. The candidate-membership rule is still applied, which is why the trigger is effective through a legitimate member: the removed node supplies only the trigger, and the receiving voter campaigns.
counterevidence: The consequence is disruption of authority rather than loss of committed data: logs, terms and entries stay consistent and the cluster elects again after the term bump.

Any cluster member can already force term changes by campaigning; what makes this path distinct is that it bypasses the voters' leader-availability protection, which normally rejects campaigns while a leader is known.
The probe delivered the request from the removed node's own transport in an in-memory cluster, which is the situation of a server taken out of the configuration but not shut down.
limitations: Measured on one three-voter in-memory cluster with the repository's own test facilities; elections are timing-dependent, so which node leads afterwards is not the decisive observation, only that leadership changed.
The removed node's request carried its own RPC header, which the handler ignores; no authentication or authorization layer outside the transport was modelled.
The account covers the transfer trigger and the vote path; it does not measure how often such churn could recur or how long the cluster stays without a leader.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled a restarted node does not load the committed configuration entries that lie at or below the commit index it recovers, and this is reproduced by two runs; the gap is bounded because a configuration entry arriving afterwards restores the node's configuration to the one in force. State, evidence and limits: restoreFromCommittedLogs clamps the store's commit index, applies the recovered range through processLogs (which ends with setLastApplied(index)), and the scan loop then starts at max(lastSnapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1, so a configuration entry at or below that index never reaches processConfigurationLogEntry. interpretations.rationale: Current account: the leader-verification quorum can be satisfied without a voter quorum, so a client that uses VerifyLeader as its staleness guard can be told a leader is still verified while every voter is unreachable. interpretations.rationale: Current account: the transfer trigger is not restricted to the current leader, and the same non-member can use it repeatedly. Evidence: the earlier receipt shows one displacement with the serving leader stepping down and the target becoming leader; the later receipt shows three consecutive rounds, each changing leadership, with the term advancing 3, 4, 5 and a leader present after every round. Mechanism from source: timeoutNow clears the known leader, sets the recipient's state to Candidate and stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer without inspecting the request's RPCHeader, so any transport-reachable peer can trigger the exchange as often as it can reach a voter; the campaign then sets LeadershipTransfer on its vote requests, and requestVote skips its leader-availability rejection when that flag is set, so voters that know a healthy leader still grant. Consequence: a removed or otherwise non-member server that remains transport-reachable can keep displacing the leader, one term per attempt, while the cluster still elects a replacement between attempts, so the effect is persistent disruption of authority rather than a stall or a loss of committed data. The measurement also corrects the account's earlier limitation, which said recurrence had not been measured.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: with RestoreCommittedLogs enabled, NewRaft's configuration scan excludes committed configuration entries. restoreFromCommittedLogs clamps the store's commit index and calls processLogs, which ends with setLastApplied(index); the following scan loop iterates from max(snapshotIndex, lastApplied)+1 up to the last log index, so any configuration entry with index at or below the recovered commit index is never passed to processConfigurationLogEntry. Both staging producers cap the staged value at entries already stored (raft.go:1266 for the leader, raft.go:1558 for followers), so the recovered commit index reaches a configuration entry whenever later entries were stored after it was committed. Consequence: the restarted node's r.configurations is the snapshot's configuration or, with no snapshot, empty, while its log reports that configuration entry as committed; an empty configuration makes runFollower abort elections (raft.go:232) and leaves the node's participant eligibility wrong until a later configuration entry or installed snapshot repairs it. Construction feedback: local, non-retained runs of these harness bytes reported variant A with last_applied_after_restart=11, config_scan_start_index=12, the bootstrap LogConfiguration at index 1 not covered and latest_config_after_restart_len=0; variant B reported the committed LogConfiguration at index 23 (adding nonvoter-B) not covered with the post-restart configuration reduced to the snapshot's single voter. Those local numbers are construction feedback only, so the conclusion stays conditional until the retained receipt of the queued experiment is read.
counterevidence: The recovered committed entries are still applied to the FSM (processLogs), and a node can still learn the current configuration from any later configuration entry or installed snapshot, so the omission can be repaired and does not by itself corrupt the FSM.

Snapshot-level configuration is loaded correctly by restoreSnapshot, so the omission only appears for configuration entries that sit between the last snapshot (or index 0) and the recovered commit index.
No captured test asserts configuration state after a RestoreCommittedLogs restart, so the captured suite neither confirms nor contradicts the omission.
limitations: The account applies only to nodes configured with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and a log store implementing CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag off, lastApplied equals the snapshot index and the scan range is unchanged.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: a RestoreCommittedLogs restart cannot complete startup recovery once the recovered committed range needs more FSM batches than the 128-slot fsmMutateCh, because runFSM is only started after the recovery work that feeds it. The receipt shows both the boundary and the mechanism. Parsed event 3 (variant committed-range-entries-6001, 94 batches): NewRaft returned in 6 ms with lastApplied 6001, i.e. the same code path completes when the range fits the buffer, and that node's configuration after restart was empty (length 0), matching the separate configuration-scan account. Parsed event 5 (variant committed-range-entries-9001, 141 batches): no return within the 20000 ms bound, and the frames captured at that moment are goroutine 10 [select] github.com/hashicorp/raft.(*Raft).processLogs.func1 -> (*Raft).processLogs(index 0x2329 = 9001) -> (*Raft).restoreFromCommittedLogs -> NewRaft, created by the harness restart goroutine. No runFSM goroutine exists for that instance, so no consumer can drain the buffer and no repair is enabled by time alone; the only escape in that select is the instance's own shutdown channel, which nothing closes during construction. Conditions: RestoreCommittedLogs enabled with a commit-tracking store, and a recovered commit index whose distance from the last applied/snapshot index exceeds 8192 authored entries (128 batches of 64) - for example a snapshot gap larger than 8192 entries on a node that crashed before the next snapshot, or a node with snapshotting disabled. Fault assumptions: none injected; the block follows from the retained history produced by the node's own commit path.
counterevidence: The observation is a 20000 ms bounded wait, so the account claims a blocked startup under the stated conditions, not an infinite block proven for all time; a caller that closes the instance's shutdown channel could release the select.

The two cases differ only in the amount of authored history (6000 versus 9000 commands) and used a single-node in-memory cluster with an InmemCommitTrackingStore and snapshotting disabled, so the boundary is a batch-capacity property of NewRaft rather than a measured property of production stores.

The blocked range here was recovered from the same node's own log without any snapshot; whether a production restart reaches a range above 8192 entries depends on snapshot cadence and crash timing, which were not measured.
limitations: Applies only when Config.RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a LogStore implementing CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag off, NewRaft never calls processLogs before starting runFSM.
The threshold is expressed in MaxAppendEntries-sized batches against the 128-slot buffer, so a configuration with a different MaxAppendEntries moves the boundary proportionally.
Interaction with the configuration-scan gap (both appear in the same recovery sequence) is not separated by this experiment; each is independently witnessed.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the empty configuration produced by a RestoreCommittedLogs restart removes the membership admission check from vote and pre-vote handling, and the retained execution shows the resulting admission of a non-member. Parsed event 6 (setup): live_config_after_restart is empty with live_voters 0 and derived_quorum_size 1, while log_recorded_config still holds the one bootstrapped voter, so the configuration in force (recorded in the node's own log) is not what the node uses. Parsed event 7 (result, same node and configuration): request_vote_granted=true with request_vote_term 3, request_prevote_granted=true with request_prevote_term 4, candidate_in_live_config=false, node_term_after_requests 3 - that is, a candidate appearing in no configuration was granted a vote and a pre-vote, and the node adopted the requester's higher term. Both declared comparisons are violated at index 7. Mechanism from source: requestVote and requestPreVote reject candidates outside the configuration only when the handler's own Servers list is non-empty, a leniency documented for the bootstrap case, so an empty list accepts any candidate; quorumSize() over the empty voter list yields 1. Consequence boundaries: the requester's log was made at least as recent as the node's, so no recency rule applied, and the restarted node has no known leader after its own recovery, so the leader-availability rejection did not apply either; the node's own election gating (runFollower aborting when no peers are known) is source-derived, not measured, and is left as the next discriminator.
counterevidence: Granting a vote when the configuration is empty is intentional behaviour for a cluster that is being bootstrapped; the defect here is that the node's own recovery path leaves the configuration empty in a cluster that is not being bootstrapped, not the leniency itself.

The probe supplied a candidate whose log was at least as recent as the node's and whose term was higher, which is what makes the vote grant observable; a stale or older candidate would still be rejected by the log-recency rules.
The same configuration gap is repaired by any later configuration entry or installed snapshot, so a healthy cluster with continuing traffic repairs the node without operator action.

interpretations.rationale: Current account (source-derived, measurement pending): a leader's commit rule is computed from r.configurations.latest, which commitment.setConfiguration and quorumSize consume; when a restart leaves that configuration behind the log's committed history, a node that then leads uses the smaller voter set for both its quorum and its replication set, so it can acknowledge a write that a majority of the configuration in force never stores, and a leader elected from that configuration can be elected without the entry. Source side: restoreFromCommittedLogs applies logs up to the recovered commit index and the configuration scan then starts after it, so the recommitted configuration entry is never loaded even though the entry recording the change remains in the log; quorumSize and commitment both count voters from the recovered configuration, and commitment.recalculate commits the (n-1)/2-th match index of that set. The discrimination is the queued experiment: it restarts the node under test from a snapshot that records a three-voter configuration while the configuration in force has five voters, transfers leadership to it, and checks whether the acknowledged write is backed by a true majority and whether it survives in a leader elected from the configuration in force. Local construction feedback of these harness bytes showed the chain end to end, including acknowledged apply error nil with only two holders out of five voters and a later leader without the payload; those local numbers are construction feedback only and are not retained evidence, so the conclusion stays conditional until the receipt is read.
counterevidence: The configuration gap needs a snapshot taken while a smaller configuration was committed plus later entries that advance the recovered commit index past the recommitting entry; a cluster that snapshots after every configuration change may not reach that state.
A later configuration entry or an installed snapshot repairs the recovered configuration, and the experiment deliberately prevents repair by isolating one voter and keeping the configuration stable.
The local construction run is not retained evidence; the phase ordering it exercises (transfer, disconnection, shutdown of holders) could behave differently under the controller's execution.
limitations: Applies to nodes with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and a LogStore implementing CommitTrackingLogStore.

The measured history is a single in-memory five-voter cluster with authored commands and the repository's in-memory stores; production stores, multi-datacenter latencies and concurrent client traffic are not covered.

The acknowledgement is observed through the Apply future of the node under test; the loss is observed as absence of the payload from the later leader's log store, which does not by itself prove that no other surviving node could later resurrect the entry.

interpretations.rationale: Current account (source-derived, probe queued): both public endpoints are pinned to zero. GetConfiguration constructs a local configurationsFuture and assigns configurations{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()}, leaving committed, committedIndex and latestIndex at their zero values, so ConfigurationFuture.Index() returns 0 although the IndexFuture contract says Index holds the index of the applied log entry; Stats then reports s["latest_configuration_index"] = future.Index(), so the documented stat key is always "0" even while s["latest_configuration"] shows the current server set. The captured tests never assert a non-zero index from this future (the only Index() assertion in the captured suite belongs to an Apply result), so nothing contradicts the reading. Local construction feedback of the queued harness reported the committed configuration entry at index 6 with future_index 0 and stats value "0" while the live configuration already contained the nonvoter; that local run is construction feedback only and is not retained evidence, so the account stays conditional until the receipt is read.
counterevidence: A zero index is harmless for callers that only read Configuration(), and GetConfiguration is documented as returning the latest configuration, which may be uncommitted; the contract violation is in the Index the future exposes and in the stat key, not in the configuration content.
The main loop still answers configurationsCh with the full configurations struct, so internal consumers such as snapshotting do see the real indices; only the client-facing future is flattened.
limitations: Observability-only impact: no consensus decision, election, or client write outcome is affected by this reading.

The declared comparison for this receipt could not be resolved because the correlation expected the setup/result pair at indices that do not carry it; the pair is present and complete at indices 15 and 16, which is what this account cites.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the configuration gap makes an acknowledged write unsafe, not merely a stale local view. Parsed event 9 records the restarted node holding the snapshot's three-voter configuration (derived quorum two) while the configuration in force has five voters and its log still holds a configuration entry beyond the snapshot; parsed event 10 records that node becoming leader through the library's own transfer API with the same three-voter configuration and a replication set of two peers; parsed event 11 records an Apply returning nil while only two nodes held the payload, below the three acknowledgements the five-voter configuration in force requires, so the assertion that the acknowledged write is backed by a true majority is violated at index 11; parsed event 12 records a leader elected from the five-voter configuration (term four) whose log store has no entry carrying the payload, so the assertion that the acknowledged write survives is violated at index 12. interpretations.rationale: Current account: the transfer trigger is not restricted to the current leader, so a non-member can displace a healthy leader. Parsed event 17 records the state before the request: the removed node is not in the configuration in force and the target is a follower. Parsed event 18 records the outcome after the removed node's TimeoutNow arrived: the target became leader, leadership_changed is true, old_leader_stepped_down is true, and the request returned no error. Both declared comparisons are violated at index 18, in a run whose exit code is 0. Mechanism from source: timeoutNow clears the known leader, sets the recipient's state to Candidate and stores candidateFromLeadershipTransfer without looking at the request's RPCHeader, so any transport-reachable peer can trigger the exchange; the election that follows sets LeadershipTransfer on its vote requests, and requestVote skips its leader-availability rejection when that flag is set, so voters that already know a healthy leader still grant. The candidate-membership rule is still applied, which is why the trigger is effective through a legitimate member: the removed node supplies only the trigger, and the receiving voter campaigns.
counterevidence: The consequence is disruption of authority rather than loss of committed data: logs, terms and entries stay consistent and the cluster elects again after the term bump.

Any cluster member can already force term changes by campaigning; what makes this path distinct is that it bypasses the voters' leader-availability protection, which normally rejects campaigns while a leader is known.
The probe delivered the request from the removed node's own transport in an in-memory cluster, which is the situation of a server taken out of the configuration but not shut down.
limitations: Measured on one three-voter in-memory cluster with the repository's own test facilities; elections are timing-dependent, so which node leads afterwards is not the decisive observation, only that leadership changed.
The removed node's request carried its own RPC header, which the handler ignores; no authentication or authorization layer outside the transport was modelled.

interpretations.rationale: Current account: the same recovered configuration that lets a stale node admit ineligible peers on some paths also makes it refuse eligible ones on the vote path. limitations: Measured on four-peer in-memory clusters with the repository's own facilities; production timings and transports are not covered.
The bound is reported for the two timer configurations used (1000 ms and the default 50 ms lease) and depends on the lease timeout, not on a fixed wall-clock constant.
Both cases isolate the leader by transport disconnection and confirm it with direct AppendEntries attempts recorded in the same events.
